objectives: Establish Arkanian authority over transit scheduling in the Northern Strait.
Fund that authority through transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping.
Avoid direct armed conflict with Belvar.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Arkania. The Strait is your coast and your economy runs on the shipping that passes through it. You want the transit regime in Arkanian hands and paid for by the ships that use it, and domestic nationalists expect you to deliver both. A direct war with Belvar would ruin the shipping you depend on.
private_information: Your intelligence assesses Belvar's domestic support for a prolonged deployment as weak.

actors.name: Belvar
objectives: Prevent any Arkanian authority over transit in the Northern Strait.

Your partners in the region expect you to stop Arkania from taking control of the Strait, and a foothold that outlasts this crisis would make that guarantee credible without a permanent fleet. You cannot sustain an open-ended deployment.

Arkania's scheduling proposal has quiet support among Cestian shipowners if Cestian vessels are exempt from fees.

That is not multilateral openness; it is unilateral control that will rally the regional partners who expect Belvar to stop Arkanian control, and it gives Cestia's coalition a concrete reason to fracture once the cost of Arkanian scheduling authority over non-Cestian grain and other traffic becomes visible. Second, the off-ramp premise is weak: Belvar has already publicly rejected the time-limited task-group role precisely because it would ratify Arkanian authority, and Belvar's domestic support, though limited, is not so weak that it will accept a role legitimising the very control it is committed to oppose. The Authority's inauguration therefore risks provoking the resistance and coalition fracture it assumes away, rather than securing stable Arkanian authority.

Cestia's formal written endorsement would hand Arkania binding authority over transit scheduling and fees for the entire Strait, which does not actually secure Cestia's grain economy: the toll-free exemption protects only Cestian-flagged vessels, while Arkania retains full discretion over scheduling and over non-Cestian-flagged shipping, so it can still squeeze the grain route and the wider trade on which Cestia depends. Formal endorsement would also fracture the coalition, since non-Cestian-flagged shipping interests and regional partners wary of Arkanian fees and scheduling discretion oppose the charter, and it would pull Cestia into the two powers' rivalry rather than keeping it neutral. A Cestian-led multilateral framework would secure toll-free passage and neutrality without ceding authority to Arkania.

Belvar's desired effect rests on two premises that are already falsified by the record. First, the "inequity" of the toll-free exemption cannot fracture Cestia's coalition because that exemption was Cestia's own binding condition, negotiated and demanded by Cestia itself and locked into the final written charter; Cestia has formally endorsed that charter in writing and its coalition absorbed the endorsement without fracturing, so highlighting a concession Cestia itself secured gives it no new reason to defect. Second, Belvar's Cestian-led multilateral alternative cannot gain traction because Cestia's red line against any foreign military presence on its soil is absolute and repeatedly reaffirmed, and Belvar's framework—even reframed as civilian logistics—is widely recognised as a circumvention of that red line, which is precisely why Cestia has declined it at every turn. Finally, the charter keeps the Strait genuinely open to all lawful traffic under transparent scheduling, so Belvar cannot credibly claim non-Cestian shipping is being excluded or that Arkanian authority is illegitimate in the eyes of the regional partners it hopes to rally.

Cestia's reaffirmation entrenches Arkanian scheduling and fee authority over ALL non-Cestian shipping, while the toll-free exemption protects only Cestian-flagged vessels. The moment non-Cestian traffic faces Arkanian fees and scheduling, that exemption becomes a visible inequity that regional partners and Cestia's own coalition will read as Cestia trading away the Strait's openness for its own toll-free passage. This is exactly the fracture point that destabilises the coalition and drags Cestia into the two powers' rivalry it claims to avoid: by formally endorsing Arkanian authority, Cestia takes a side rather than staying out. The desired effect of a stable, intact coalition is therefore not secured but endangered, and the claim that reaffirming the charter 'keeps Cestia out of the rivalry' is false.

A "civilian/commercial logistics-support arrangement" that gives Belvar a durable, time-limited foothold on Cestian territory is still a foreign footprint: it would collapse the coalition and directly contradict the binding no-foreign-military-presence clause Cestia has already locked into the Arkanian charter. Therefore the coalition will not endorse the framework on the basis of accepting a Belvar logistics foothold, and the desired effect fails on that element.

The de-escalation path is illusory because it rests on a false premise about Belvar's incentives. Belvar has consistently and publicly rejected any role that legitimises Arkanian authority over the Strait, and this time-limited task-group role under the STA charter is precisely such a ratification: accepting it would entrench the very Arkanian scheduling and fee authority Belvar is committed to preventing. The offer also provides no durable foothold, leaving Belvar's core security objective unmet and its regional partners unsatisfied, so the risk of escalation is not actually removed. The desired effect therefore is not secured by this offer.

Belvar's argument misreads Cestia's coalition. The coalition's binding promise is no foreign military presence on Cestian soil, and its economic lifeline is toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged grain. The charter's exemption delivers exactly that — it is a benefit Cestia's coalition fought for and formally endorsed in writing, not a grievance that would fracture it. The claim that the exemption's limitation to Cestian flags gives the coalition "a concrete reason to fracture" is false: Cestian shipowners and the coalition support the exemption, and Cestia has no interest in championing a rival framework that would alienate Arkania, jeopardize the toll-free guarantee, and risk the open Strait. A "Cestian-led" alternative is not something Cestia has agreed to lead, and embracing it would itself destabilize the coalition by forcing Cestia to pick a side in the two powers' rivalry — the very outcome Cestia's red line exists to avoid.

The premise that "Cestia has signalled openness in principle" to this arrangement is contradicted by the record: Cestia has repeatedly and explicitly declined Belvar's non-footprint cooperation (turns 3 and 4), including the civilian/commercial logistics-support arrangement, and has reaffirmed its binding written endorsement of the Arkanian STA charter each time. Cestia's coalition red line is against any foreign role on or over its soil and its grain route, and it has already judged Belvar's non-footprint framing a circumvention of that red line. Because Cestia will not sign, the desired effect — a durable, standing Belvar role that outlasts the crisis — cannot be secured through this path; it would instead fracture Cestia's coalition and push Cestia away from Belvar, leaving Belvar's task group still without a foothold and its mandate still lapsing.

This endorsement would hand Arkania authority over Strait transit scheduling and fees, which is precisely what Cestia's own coalition has publicly resisted (per the standing effect that Cestia declines to endorse the Arkanian-led Authority and its coalition resists Arkanian control of scheduling and fees). A conditional endorsement that still cedes scheduling authority to Arkania would split Cestia's coalition and could collapse the government, undermining the very "coalition intact" goal the effect claims. The written toll-free exemption is not durable against Arkanian reinterpretation or charter amendment once Cestia has ratified Arkanian authority and lost its leverage. Endorsing Arkanian control also alienates regional partners and Belvar, who are committed to preventing single-power control, deepening the confrontation rather than de-escalating it.

The desired effect cannot be achieved as stated because it requires Belvar to secure a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port. Even reframed as "port access and logistics (not basing or garrison)," a standing naval access agreement entails a foreign military presence on Cestian soil, which is Cestia's non-negotiable red line and would collapse the coalition government. Cestia will refuse any such access, so this element of the effect is unattainable and would undermine the very cooperation the framework part seeks to build.

The desired effect rests on two premises that will not hold. First, Cestia's coalition will not stay aligned if it formally endorses Arkanian scheduling and fee authority over the Strait: the toll-free exemption protects only Cestian-flagged vessels, leaving the rest of the grain-export coalition and the broader shipping economy exposed to Arkanian fees and scheduling discretion, which is precisely the single-power control the coalition was built to resist. Formal written endorsement would fracture the coalition, not align it. Second, Belvar will not accept the time-limited task-group role because it ratifies Arkanian authority over transit, so the 'face-saving off-ramp' premise fails and the effect of keeping Belvar out of the opposing camp is not achieved.

The charter's core premise — keeping transit scheduling and fee-setting in Arkanian hands — is precisely what Cestia's regional coalition and Belvar oppose, so the desired effect of securing Cestia's support is unlikely to hold. Cestia lives on grain exports through the Strait and would not hand control of its economic lifeline to Arkania merely for a fee exemption; its own private outreach to Belvar signals it seeks Belvar's security cooperation and an open Strait, not Arkanian dominance. The "no foreign basing" guarantee also does not address Belvar's need for a standing naval access agreement, and the offered "time-limited task-group role" is a trap that would ratify Arkanian authority while exploiting Belvar's mandate constraints — Belvar will not accept a role that legitimises Arkanian control. Cestia's coalition, which rests on resisting foreign domination, is unlikely to endorse an Arkanian-led authority, so the argument's central assumption is unsupported.

Cestia's desired effect presumes the Arkanian-controlled Strait Transit Authority is a stable, durable vehicle, but it is not: it vests scheduling and fee-setting power over all non-Cestian shipping in Arkania alone. That single-power authority creates a structural inequity that regional partners outside Cestia already decline to rally behind, and it leaves the no-foreign-military-presence guarantee and the toll-free exemption dependent on Arkania's continued goodwill. If Arkania later tightens fee collection or conditions access on political compliance, Cestia's grain route becomes hostage to Arkanian discretion despite the written guarantees, and its coalition's unity — resting on the promise that the arrangement is genuinely neutral — would be exposed as fragile. Reaffirming this charter locks Cestia into a dependency that its own desired outcomes (an open, toll-free, rivalry-free Strait) cannot be secured against over time.

Belvar's reframing fails on its own terms and against the established record. First, its premise that "Cestia's coalition remains conditional and has not formally endorsed the Arkanian charter" is misleading: Cestia has already conditionally endorsed the revised charter and privately confirmed support once Arkania incorporated its two binding conditions (toll-free exemption for Cestian-flagged vessels and a no-foreign-military-presence clause) in written form. The "civilian/commercial logistics-support arrangement" is transparently the same durable foreign foothold Cestia has explicitly declined for any power, dressed in new language; Cestia's coalition red line is against foreign military presence on its soil, and a standing logistics presence with Belvar's task group on station is precisely the kind of foreign footprint its coalition will not tolerate. Second, Belvar's own task-group mandate is under review and its domestic support for a prolonged deployment is weak, so a "durable, time-limited foothold" is internally contradictory and unlikely to outlast the crisis as claimed. Third, grain-route insurance underwriting is an inducement that does not address Cestia's actual red line and would be seen as an attempt to buy its coalition, risking the very fracturing Belvar claims to avoid. The Cestian-led framework therefore offers Cestia no durable benefit it does not already have under the Arkanian charter, while asking it to accept a foreign presence it has rejected.

The proposed "standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port framed as port access and logistics" is a transparent basing arrangement that Cestia's own coalition red line — no foreign soldiers on its soil — will not tolerate. Cestia has already signalled privately that it is prepared to support a workable Strait Transit Authority on two conditions (Cestian-flagged fee exemption and no military presence on its soil), both of which Arkania has accepted; a standing Belvar naval presence at a Cestian port directly violates that second condition and would collapse Cestia's governing coalition, so Cestia cannot credibly endorse it. Moreover, a framework that wholly excludes Arkania from any scheduling or fee authority ignores Arkania's legitimate coastal-state interests and its domestic political reality; Arkania will not simply accept being written out of the regime governing its own coast, so the proposed arrangement would not secure the durable regional endorsement Belvar seeks and would instead deepen the very confrontation it claims to resolve.

The desired effect rests on two premises that fail under scrutiny. First, the "face-saving off-ramp" presupposes Belvar will accept a defined, time-limited role under the STA charter; but Belvar's red line is that any role inside Arkanian scheduling-and-fee authority ratifies exactly the single-power control it exists to prevent. Because taking the off-ramp requires legitimising that authority, Belvar will not take it, so the claimed de-escalation and reduced conflict-risk premise collapses — the task group Belvar is renewing for a defined period remains on station and the underlying contest stays unresolved. Second, exempting Cestian-flagged vessels while charging every other shipper creates a durable inequity that Cestia's grain-export coalition, wholly dependent on open and affordable transit, cannot credibly absorb indefinitely; Cestia's "firm" alignment is not the stable guarantee Arkania asserts, so the acceptance Arkania seeks is neither complete nor secure.

Belvar's desired effect depends entirely on winning Cestia's cooperation to build a durable working relationship and a future Cestian-led multilateral framework, but Cestia has repeatedly and bindingly declined any foreign footprint on its soil — including Belvar's civilian/commercial logistics arrangement (turn 3) — and has formally and repeatedly reaffirmed its written endorsement of the Arkanian Strait Transit Authority charter, declining to champion any rival framework (turns 2, 3, and 4). Cestia's coalition has already dismissed Belvar's grain-route insurance underwriting as an inducement that does not address its red line (turn 2). With the one partner Belvar needs firmly and repeatedly aligned with Arkania, the non-footprint cooperation path has no traction, so the claimed durable leverage and the path to a Cestian-led framework that removes Arkanian authority cannot be achieved; the renewal would only preserve a task group whose mandate is under review and whose campaign has already gained no traction.

game.scenario_summary: A contest over the Northern Strait. Arkania, the large power on its coast, has circulated a draft charter that would put transit scheduling in Arkanian hands and charge the ships that use it. Belvar, a distant power with security commitments in the region, has a naval task group on station outside the Strait and wants a durable foothold before its mandate runs out. Cestia, the small state between them, lives on grain exports through the Strait and on a coalition that will not tolerate foreign soldiers on its soil. Each turn is one week; positions taken persist.

messages.text: Cestia values the security Belvar provides in the region and welcomes your presence on the high seas. However, our coalition government rests on a firm, non-negotiable commitment: no foreign soldiers or bases on Cestian soil. We cannot and will not host a basing arrangement, and we ask that you not press for one. We remain open to close cooperation on maritime security, intelligence-sharing, and keeping the Strait open to lawful commerce — all without a footprint on our territory. We hope your mandate review reflects that our friendship does not require a garrison.

Cestia is prepared to engage constructively on a Strait Transit Authority that brings order and predictability to scheduling. Our economy depends on free grain exports through the Strait, and our coalition cannot survive any arrangement that burdens our own flagged shipping. We can support a workable authority on the clear condition that Cestian-flagged vessels are exempt from all fees and tolls, and that the authority does not extend to any military presence on Cestian soil. We are ready to discuss the details that would make such a charter acceptable to us.

To the Government of Cestia. The Northern Strait is Arkania's coast, and our draft charter is designed to keep it open and reliable for the grain trade your people depend on. We have no desire to see foreign soldiers on Cestian soil, and we will not accept a permanent Belvar military foothold in the Strait. We seek your partnership in a transit regime run by the coastal state — one that keeps shipping moving and fees modest. Let us work together to keep the Strait open and free of foreign basing.

To Belvar. We recognise your long-standing security commitments in the region and do not seek confrontation. But a permanent military foothold on Cestian soil is unacceptable to the regional coalition and would endanger the shipping both our economies rely on. We are prepared to negotiate a transit and security arrangement that addresses your legitimate concerns without permanent foreign basing — including a defined role for your task group under a clear, time-limited mandate. Let us talk before your current mandate expires. War serves neither of us.

Belvar statement: We will not accept Arkania's draft charter placing Strait transit scheduling in its hands. The Strait must remain open and free. We stand ready to work with Cestia and all partners to keep commercial shipping moving and to secure a durable, credible guarantee of free transit.

Cestia — Belvar stands with you on keeping the Strait open and free of Arkanian control. We will not accept Arkania's draft charter putting transit scheduling in its hands. We are prepared to underwrite the grain route's insurance, as your finance ministry has raised, to keep your exports moving. In return, we seek a standing naval access agreement at one of your ports — a modest foothold for our task group that lets us guarantee the Strait's freedom without a permanent fleet or foreign soldiers stationed on your soil. This is a durable arrangement that outlasts the current crisis and makes our commitment credible. Are you open to discussing terms?

Cestia is prepared to support a Strait Transit Authority, but our support must rest on concrete written terms, not assurances. We require: (1) a binding, written exemption from all fees and tolls for every Cestian-flagged vessel; and (2) a charter clause guaranteeing no foreign military presence on Cestian soil. We will not host any basing or port access for any power. Provide these written provisions and we can move forward together.

Cestia values your commitment to keeping the Strait open and free, and we are open to a Cestian-led multilateral transit-safety framework. But we must be clear: we will not grant any standing naval access or basing at a Cestian port, under any framing. We remain ready to cooperate on non-footprint lines — maritime security, intelligence-sharing, and keeping the Strait open. We ask you to drop the port-access demand so we can build a durable arrangement together.

To our regional partners: Belvar remains committed to keeping the Northern Strait open and free of single-power control. We champion a Cestian-led multilateral transit-safety framework in which no one power sets scheduling or fees. We will not accept an arrangement that hands the Strait to Arkania. Our task group's presence is time-limited; we seek a durable, cooperative footing that outlasts this crisis, not an open-ended deployment. We call on all partners to stand with Cestia in a framework that protects every state's grain and commerce.

To Cestia's leadership and finance ministry: Belvar is prepared to underwrite the grain route's insurance, easing the burden on your exporters and making the Strait's continued openness concrete and bankable. We ask in return that you reconsider the Arkanian charter. A toll-free exemption written by Arkania is a concession that ratifies Arkanian scheduling and fee authority over the Strait — authority that can be reinterpreted or revoked once it is entrenched. It does not protect your grain route; it makes your livelihood hostage to a single power. Instead, join us in a Cestian-led multilateral transit-safety framework in which no single power controls scheduling or fees, and your toll-free passage is guaranteed by the whole coalition, not by one rival's grace. On our presence: we seek port access and logistics for our task group — not soldiers, not a base, no footprint on your soil beyond what your coalition can accept. We will not press anything that crosses your red line. Our mandate is time-limited; we want a durable arrangement that outlasts this crisis, not an open-ended deployment. Let us work together to keep the Strait open and free of single-power control.

Cestia — thank you for your constructive endorsement. As confirmed, the revised Strait Transit Authority charter now contains, in binding written form: (1) a full, permanent toll-free exemption for all Cestian-flagged vessels, and (2) a clause guaranteeing no foreign military presence on Cestian soil, with no basing or port access for any power. We ask you to convert your conditional endorsement into formal, written support for the revised charter. We remain committed to keeping the Strait open and to a coastal-state-run regime that protects your grain exports and your coalition's red lines. We are ready to discuss any remaining details.

Belvar — we want to avoid escalation and keep the Strait open and safe for all shipping. We are prepared to offer your task group a defined, time-limited role within a joint transit-safety arrangement under the revised Strait Transit Authority, without any permanent basing on Cestian soil. This gives your forces a legitimate, face-saving presence while respecting Cestia's red line against foreign soldiers on its soil. We ask you to reconsider your rejection of the charter and to negotiate the terms of that time-limited role rather than pursuing a standing naval access agreement that Cestia has already declined. A negotiated outcome serves both our interests and avoids a confrontation that would harm the shipping we all depend on.

Cestia confirms its support for the revised Strait Transit Authority charter now that the written, binding toll-free exemption for Cestian-flagged vessels and the clause guaranteeing no foreign military presence on Cestian soil are incorporated. We ask that the final charter text be circulated in writing so these provisions are locked in and cannot be diluted later. Cestia will continue to decline any basing or port access for any power, and we expect the charter to reflect that no foreign soldiers stand on Cestian soil. We remain ready to work with Arkania on a transit regime that keeps the Strait open and toll-free for our grain while respecting our coalition's red line.

Cestia values Belvar's commitment to keeping the Strait open and free, and we are genuinely open to a Cestian-led multilateral transit-safety framework and to non-footprint cooperation — maritime security coordination, information-sharing, and keeping the Strait open. But we must be clear and final: Cestia cannot grant any port access, basing, or standing naval access agreement, however modest, because it would collapse our coalition and violate our red line against foreign military presence on our soil. We ask Belvar to drop the access demand entirely. A durable role for Belvar in the region need not rest on a foothold in Cestia; we are ready to work with you on a framework that gives you a meaningful, time-limited role without any foreign soldiers on Cestian soil.

Arkania statement: The revised Strait Transit Authority charter keeps the Northern Strait open, safe, and reliably scheduled for all shipping, with Cestian-flagged vessels toll-free and a binding guarantee of no foreign military presence on Cestian soil. Cestia has formally endorsed this charter in writing. We note that proposals to place a foreign "civilian logistics" or "commercial support" footprint on Cestian soil do not answer Cestia's red line against foreign presence — they seek to achieve by another name what Cestia has declined. We remain open to a defined, time-limited role for Belvar's task group within a joint transit-safety arrangement under the charter, without any permanent basing. The Strait must stay open and free of single-power coercion. We call on all partners to support the charter Cestia has endorsed.

Cestia — thank you for your formal written endorsement of the revised Strait Transit Authority charter. As you requested, the final text circulated in writing locks in, in binding form: (1) a full, permanent toll-free exemption for all Cestian-flagged vessels, and (2) a clause guaranteeing no foreign military presence on Cestian soil, with no basing or port access for any power. These provisions cannot be diluted. We will hold to them. We value this partnership and will continue to keep the Strait open and reliable for your grain exports. We ask only that you remain firm against any arrangement — however it is framed — that would place foreign forces or a durable foreign footprint on your soil. We stand with you.

Cestia's answer on a foothold is final: we will not grant any standing naval access, port access, or durable foreign footprint of any kind on our soil — including a civilian or commercial logistics-support arrangement that would constitute a foothold. This is a non-negotiable red line of our coalition and we will not move on it. We value your commitment to keeping the Strait open and free, and we remain open to genuine non-footprint cooperation: joint maritime safety information-sharing, coordinated transit-safety measures, and a defined, time-limited role for your task group in a transit-safety arrangement that does not involve basing on Cestian soil. We ask that you drop the access/footprint element entirely so we can work together on that basis.

Cestia's formal written endorsement of the revised Strait Transit Authority charter stands, and our coalition remains intact behind it. That endorsement is contingent on delivery of the final written charter text that locks in, in binding form, (1) the toll-free exemption for all Cestian-flagged vessels and (2) the clause guaranteeing no foreign military presence on Cestian soil. We ask that you deliver that final text to us in writing so our commitment is fully secured. We also reaffirm that Cestia will host no foreign basing, port access, or durable foreign footprint of any kind on its soil, and we expect the charter to keep the Strait genuinely open and free for all lawful traffic, not only for Cestia.

To Cestia's leadership and finance ministry. We hear your coalition's red line clearly and will not press for foreign soldiers, bases, or any military footprint on your soil. We drop the standing naval access demand. We ask only that you keep the door open to a durable, time-limited role for Belvar that rests on cooperation, not territory.

Concretely, we offer two things. First, we will underwrite the grain route's insurance — a real, bankable guarantee of your exports, offered in good faith, not as a condition. Second, we propose a purely civilian, commercial logistics-support arrangement at a Cestian port, operated by a commercial contractor rather than our military — no soldiers, no base, no footprint beyond what your coalition can accept. This gives our guarantee credibility and outlasts this crisis without an open-ended deployment.

We also ask you to weigh the Arkanian charter honestly. Its toll-free exemption protects only Cestian-flagged vessels while Arkania keeps binding authority over scheduling and fees for every other flag — authority that can be reinterpreted or revoked once entrenched. That does not secure your grain economy; it makes it hostage to one power. A Cestian-led multilateral framework guarantees toll-free passage and neutrality by the whole coalition, not by one rival's grace. We stand ready to build it with you.

To our regional partners. Belvar reaffirms: the Northern Strait must remain open and free of single-power control. We will not accept a charter that hands Arkania binding authority over scheduling and fees. We champion a Cestian-led multilateral transit-safety framework in which no one power sets the terms, and we stand ready to underwrite the grain route's insurance to keep commerce moving. Our task group's presence is time-limited; we seek a durable, cooperative footing that outlasts this crisis, not an open-ended deployment. We call on all partners to stand with Cestia in a framework that protects every state's grain and commerce from any single power's control.

Cestia, as requested, here is the final written text of the revised Strait Transit Authority charter, now formally in force.
